text: # COVID-19 (Coronavirus): Public Health Guidance ## Overview COVID-19 is an infectious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus. It primarily spreads through airborne respiratory droplets and smaller aerosols when an infected individual breathes, speaks, coughs, or sneezes. The disease ranges from mild cold-like symptoms to severe viral pneumonia and acute respiratory distress. ## COVID-19 Vaccine Names and Types Multiple vaccines have been approved by global health authorities (including the WHO, FDA, and EMA) to prevent severe COVID-19: 1. **Pfizer-BioNTech (Comirnaty)**: An mRNA vaccine encoding the viral spike protein, approved for primary series and updated seasonal boosters. 2. **Moderna (Spikevax)**: An mRNA vaccine using lipid nanoparticle technology, widely authorized for children and adults. 3. **Novavax (Nuvaxovid / Covovax)**: A protein subunit vaccine with a saponin-based adjuvant (Matrix-M), providing an alternative to mRNA technology. 4. **Oxford-AstraZeneca (Vaxzevria / Covishield)**: A recombinant adenovirus vector vaccine. 5. **Johnson & Johnson (Janssen)**: A single-dose adenovirus vector vaccine (Ad26.COV2.S). 6. **Bharat Biotech (Covaxin)**: An inactivated whole-virion coronavirus vaccine. 7. **Sinovac (CoronaVac)** and **Sinopharm (BBIBP-CorV)**: Inactivated virus vaccines widely used globally. ## Vaccination and Boosters Vaccination is the most effective intervention to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. - **Immunity Timeline**: Substantial antibody protection develops approximately 10 to 14 days following vaccination. - **Boosters**: Because the virus evolves and antibodies decline over time, updated seasonal booster shots tailored to recent circulating variants (such as Omicron sublineages) are recommended, particularly for older adults, healthcare personnel, and individuals with underlying health conditions. ## Symptoms

- **Boosters**: Because the virus evolves and antibodies decline over time, updated seasonal booster shots tailored to recent circulating variants (such as Omicron sublineages) are recommended, particularly for older adults, healthcare personnel, and individuals with underlying health conditions. ## Symptoms Common COVID-19 symptoms include fever or chills, dry cough, shortness of breath, sudden loss of taste or smell (anosmia), extreme fatigue, body aches, headache, sore throat, and nasal congestion. Symptoms typically emerge 2 to 14 days after exposure. ## When to Seek Emergency Medical Attention Seek immediate emergency medical care if you observe red-flag symptoms: trouble breathing, persistent pain or pressure in the chest, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, gray, or blue-colored skin, lips, or nail beds. ## Everyday Prevention Measures In addition to vaccination, transmission risk is significantly reduced by improving indoor ventilation, wearing high-filtration masks (such as N95 or KN95 respirators) in crowded spaces, practicing frequent hand hygiene with soap or alcohol-based sanitizer, and isolating when symptomatic.

# Hand Hygiene and Everyday Infection Prevention ## Why Hand Hygiene Matters Hands are the most common vehicle for transferring germs from surfaces to
the eyes, nose and mouth. Proper hand hygiene reduces respiratory infections
such as colds and influenza, gastrointestinal infections, and the spread of
antimicrobial-resistant organisms in both community and healthcare settings. ## Correct Handwashing Technique 1. Wet hands with clean running water (warm or cold). 2. Apply soap and lather by rubbing palms together. 3. Scrub for at least 20 seconds, covering the backs of the hands, between
   the fingers, under the nails, and the thumbs. 4. Rinse thoroughly under running water. 5. Dry with a clean towel or air-dry. Twenty seconds is roughly the time needed to hum the "Happy Birthday" song
twice. Antibacterial soap is not required; ordinary soap works by lifting
germs and dirt off the skin mechanically. ## Hand Sanitiser Alcohol-based hand rubs containing at least 60 percent alcohol are an
acceptable substitute when soap and water are unavailable. Apply enough gel
to cover all hand surfaces and rub until dry, which takes about 20 to 30
seconds. Sanitiser is less effective than washing when hands are visibly
dirty or greasy, and it does not reliably inactivate certain stomach
viruses such as norovirus. ## Respiratory Etiquette Cough or sneeze into a tissue or the inner elbow, never into bare hands. Dispose of tissues immediately and wash hands afterwards. Wearing a
well-fitting mask in crowded indoor spaces during respiratory illness
seasons further reduces droplet transmission. ## Surface Cleaning Frequently touched surfaces such as door handles, light switches, phones,
keyboards and toys should be cleaned regularly with household detergent and
disinfected when someone in the household is ill. Bleach-based disinfectants
are effective against most respiratory and gastrointestinal viruses when
used according to the label. ## When Hygiene Alone Is Not Enough

vaccines exist, nor medical evaluation when symptoms are severe. Fever with
difficulty breathing, symptoms lasting beyond ten days, or dehydration in
young children always warrant professional assessment.

# Seasonal Influenza: Public Health Guidance ## Overview Seasonal influenza (the flu) is an acute respiratory infection caused by
influenza viruses. It spreads mainly through respiratory droplets released
when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks, and less often through
contaminated surfaces. Most people recover within one to two weeks without
medical treatment, but certain groups are at higher risk of severe illness. ## Symptoms Typical symptoms appear suddenly and include fever, chills, muscle and joint
pain, headache, sore throat, dry cough and severe tiredness. Fever usually
lasts three to five days. Children may also experience gastrointestinal
symptoms such as nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, which are uncommon in adults. ## Contagious Period An adult with influenza is contagious from about one day before symptoms
begin until five to seven days after onset. Children and people with weakened
immune systems can shed the virus for longer, sometimes more than ten days. The highest viral shedding usually coincides with the fever period, which is
why staying home until 24 hours after the fever resolves without
fever-reducing medication is recommended. ## Vaccination Annual vaccination is the most effective way to prevent influenza. The
vaccine is reformulated each year to match circulating strains. When the
match is good, vaccination reduces the risk of flu illness by approximately
40 to 60 percent in the general population. Immunity takes about two weeks
to develop after vaccination. Vaccination is especially important for
pregnant women, adults over 65, young children, and people with chronic
conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease. ## When to Seek Medical Care Most cases can be managed at home with rest and fluids. Seek medical care
promptly if there is difficulty breathing, chest pain, persistent high fever
beyond three days, confusion, signs of dehydration, or if symptoms improve
and then return with a worse cough and fever, which can signal a secondary
bacterial infection such as pneumonia.

water for at least 20 seconds, use alcohol-based hand sanitiser with at

# Healthy Sleep: Guidance for Adults ## Recommended Amounts Adults aged 18 to 64 should aim for seven to nine hours of sleep per night. Adults over 65 need seven to eight hours. Consistency matters as much as
duration: going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, including
weekends, strengthens the body clock. ## Why Sleep Matters During sleep the brain consolidates memory, clears metabolic waste, and
regulates the hormones controlling appetite, stress and growth. Regularly
sleeping less than seven hours is associated with impaired concentration and
mood, weakened immune response, weight gain, and elevated risk of
hypertension, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. ## Common Sleep Disorders Insomnia, the difficulty falling or staying asleep despite adequate
opportunity, is the most common sleep complaint and is often driven by
stress, irregular schedules, caffeine, or screens before bed. Obstructive
sleep apnoea, in which breathing repeatedly stops during sleep, causes
unrefreshing sleep, loud snoring and daytime sleepiness, and raises blood
pressure and heart risk. Restless legs syndrome and shift-work disorder are
further common causes of poor sleep. ## Practical Sleep Hygiene - Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool, around 18 degrees Celsius. - Stop caffeine at least six hours before bedtime. - Avoid large meals, alcohol and intense exercise close to bedtime. - Put screens away one hour before bed; the light and engagement delay
  sleep onset. - Get bright daylight in the morning, which anchors the circadian rhythm. - Use the bed only for sleep; if awake longer than 20 minutes, get up and
  do something calm in dim light until sleepy. ## When to Seek Help Consult a healthcare provider if snoring is loud with pauses in breathing,
if daytime sleepiness interferes with work or driving, if insomnia persists
beyond a few weeks, or if sleep problems began alongside low mood or
anxiety.
